frontmatter.confidence: grounded (consensus citation); inferred (AI-specific framing); unverified (2026 migration endpoint)

What it does.markdown:
Akash is a decentralized marketplace for compute capacity: tenants publish a
deployment manifest describing what they need (CPU, GPU, storage), independent
providers bid competitively to host it, and the lowest qualifying bid wins. It
started as general-purpose cloud compute and has since leaned heavily into
GPU/AI workloads as that demand grew.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Historically an application-specific **Cosmos SDK** chain using **Tendermint**
  Byzantine-fault-tolerant consensus (Proof-of-Stake) to handle escrow, leases,
  and provider payouts on-chain, while the actual compute runs off-chain on
  provider hardware (Docker/Kubernetes-based).
- **Reverse auction** is the core marketplace mechanism: tenants set terms,
  providers compete on price, settlement is in AKT.
- **GPU marketplace** ("Supercloud") shipped via Mainnet 6, August 2023;
  supports H100/A100/A6000/RTX4090/L40S across 150+ providers as of 2026.
  ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/akash-gpu-marketplace-ai-compute/))
- **AkashML**, launched Nov 22 2025, adds a managed AI-inference layer with an
  OpenAI-compatible API that routes inference requests across available GPU
  providers on the network. ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/akash-network-2026-gpu-market-leaves-cosmos/))
- **2026 base-chain migration (unverified endpoint, in progress):** per AEP-79,
  Akash is deprecating its sovereign Cosmos-SDK chain in favor of a
  "shared-security" model — buying BFT security from an established L1 rather
  than running its own validator set — driven by (a) capital inefficiency of
  self-staking and (b) a 2025 Cosmos SDK licensing change (Apache 2.0 →
  Source Available Evaluation License for the Enterprise module) that forced
  the issue. ~15 L1 candidates were evaluated; Solana was reported as the
  leading contender as of this research pass; migration targeted for Q4 2026.
  Not independently confirmed against Akash's own roadmap page beyond the
  secondary source below — reverify before treating "Solana" as settled.
  ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/akash-network-2026-gpu-market-leaves-cosmos/),
  [akash.network/roadmap/aep-79](https://akash.network/roadmap/aep-79/))

frontmatter.name: Allora Network
frontmatter.field: Decentralized ML forecasting / inference incentive networks
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (architecture/status facts); no external academic lineage found

What it does.markdown:
Allora is a decentralized network (a "Model Coordination Network") where
many independent ML models submit predictions/inferences on a given
topic; the network combines them into a single synthesized inference
that is intended to outperform any single contributing model, and pays
contributors based on the measured quality of their individual
contribution to that combined result.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Built on the **Cosmos SDK**, using **CometBFT** as the underlying BFT
  consensus engine, with a **Delegated Proof-of-Stake (DPoS)** validator
  set securing the chain itself (this part is standard Cosmos-chain
  infrastructure, not Allora-specific).
- Allora-specific layer on top: **Workers** submit inferences/forecasts
  on a "topic"; **Reputers** stake-weight and score those submissions
  for accuracy; the network combines scored submissions into a single
  output via Allora's own **"Inference Synthesis"** mechanism.
- Rewards are distributed based on each participant's measured marginal
  contribution to the synthesized result, not raw output volume — intended
  to reward genuinely useful predictions over ones that just add noise.
- Mainnet (with the ALLO token) launched 2025-11-11, per Allora
  Foundation's own announcement
  ([allora.network/blog/allora-foundation-announces-launch-of-allora-mainnet-and-allo-token](https://www.allora.network/blog/allora-foundation-announces-launch-of-allora-mainnet-and-allo-token)).
  ALLO launched across multiple chains (Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain) in
  addition to Allora's own L1.

frontmatter.name: Apple Private Cloud Compute (PCC)
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (architecture); no academic paper lineage — see Known limitations

What it does.markdown:
Private Cloud Compute (PCC) lets Apple Intelligence offload AI requests that
need more capability than an on-device model can provide, to Apple's own
servers, while keeping the same privacy guarantee as on-device processing.
Per Apple's own description: "Personal user data sent to PCC isn't accessible
to anyone other than the user — not even to Apple."
([security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute](https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/))

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Hardware root of trust**: custom-built Apple silicon server hardware
  carrying the same Secure Enclave and Secure Boot technology used in
  iPhone/iPad. Certificates are rooted in each node's Secure Enclave UID.
- **Attestation**: before a device sends encrypted request data, it
  cryptographically verifies the target PCC node's attestation. Requests
  bypass load balancers and encrypt directly to the validated node.
- **Physical/manufacturing verification**: high-resolution imaging and
  tamper switches activated before sealing; data-center validation involves
  multiple independent Apple teams plus third-party observation.
- **Multi-vendor attestation**: for components whose compromise could
  exfiltrate data, attestation is rooted in at least two independent
  hardware vendors (Apple's own hardware plus, for some components, Google
  Cloud) rather than a single vendor's root of trust.
- **Stateless / no-retention design**: the Secure Enclave randomizes the
  data-volume encryption key on every reboot without persisting it;
  request-associated data is deleted on completion; address space is
  periodically recycled; there is no remote shell or interactive debugging
  interface into production nodes.
- **Public verifiability**: every production PCC software build's
  measurement is written to an append-only, cryptographically tamper-proof
  transparency log; binary images are published for independent inspection
  within 90 days; a Virtual Research Environment and source releases
  (the CloudAttestation and Thimble projects) let outside researchers
  verify the published software matches what's actually running.
- **Request anonymization (separate from the confidentiality claim above)**:
  RSA Blind Signatures (IETF RFC 9474) and an Oblivious HTTP relay (RFC 9458)
  are used so that request routing can't be linked back to a specific
  device/identity — this is about non-targetability, not about protecting
  the content of the request itself.

Source for all of the above:
[security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute](https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/)
and [security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research](https://security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research/).

frontmatter.name: Azure Confidential AI
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (ledger lineage); inferred/vendor-spec (TEE hardware lineage)

What it does.markdown:
Microsoft's umbrella term for running AI training/inference inside
hardware-isolated Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) on Azure, so
that neither Microsoft (the cloud operator) nor other tenants can see
model weights or input data while the workload runs — and, in the
newer "Confidential Inferencing" variant, producing an auditable record
of exactly what code ran.

**Caution:** Microsoft has published more than one architecture under
this umbrella, and they are not identical (see below) — this entry
documents what was actually found for each, rather than collapsing them
into one story.

Architecture summary.markdown:
**1. Azure confidential VMs (the base layer)** — grounded directly from
Microsoft Learn (learn.microsoft.com/azure/confidential-computing/confidential-vm-overview):
- CPU TEE via AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX, hardware-enforced isolation from
  the hypervisor/host.
- A dedicated virtual TPM (vTPM, TPM 2.0 spec) per VM for attestation
  and key/secret storage.
- Boot-time attestation via Azure Attestation; the VM won't start if
  required isolation settings (e.g. SEV-SNP) aren't enabled.
- GPU confidential computing extension: the `NCCadsH100v5` VM series
  pairs SEV-SNP with NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU confidential-computing
  mode, forming one TEE spanning CPU and GPU, with encrypted PCIe
  traffic between them.
- Secure key release: Azure Key Vault Managed HSM can be configured to
  release decryption keys only after Azure Attestation confirms the VM
  state.

frontmatter.name: Bittensor
frontmatter.field: Decentralized incentive / consensus mechanisms for ML networks
frontmatter.confidence: grounded

What it does.markdown:
Bittensor is a decentralized network in which independent operators ("miners")
run machine-learning models and are paid in the TAO token based on how
useful their outputs are judged to be by other network participants
("validators"). Instead of a central benchmark deciding what's useful, peers
rank each other, and rewards flow from that peer-ranking.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Subtensor**: the layer-0 blockchain (built on Polkadot Substrate) that
  records peer identity, stake, and the consensus/incentive state.
- **Subnets**: independently defined competitions, each specifying its own
  task (e.g. text generation, image generation) and its own validator
  scoring logic. As of 2026 the network has scaled to roughly 64-128 active
  subnets (sources disagree on the exact figure at time of writing; mainnet
  slot cap is 128, with an expansion to 256 planned). [[FalconX: State of
  Bittensor]](https://www.falconx.io/newsroom/state-of-bittensor-subnet-adoption-trends-network-mechanics-and-covenants-departure)
- **Dynamic TAO (dTAO)**: deployed to mainnet ~Feb 13, 2025. Replaced a
  single global emission pool with per-subnet "alpha" tokens and AMM pools,
  letting TAO holders stake directly into specific subnets rather than the
  network as a whole. [[CryptoBriefing]](https://cryptobriefing.com/bittensor-dynamic-tao-emission-model/)
- **Yuma Consensus (YC)**: the mechanism that turns validator rankings into
  miner payouts (see below).

Built on (foundational lineage).markdown:
**Shapley (1952), "A Value for n-Person Games"** — explicitly cited in
Bittensor's own academic paper, *"Incentivizing Intelligence: The Bittensor
Approach"* (Steeves, Shaabana, Hu, Luus, Liu, Tasker-Steeves et al.), hosted
at [bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia), as the
theoretical basis for the peer-ranking mechanism: Shapley values are used to
fairly attribute each peer's contribution to the network's informational
output across permutations of participants.

The whitepaper (*"Bittensor: A Peer-to-Peer Intelligence Market,"* Yuma Rao,
[bittensor.com/whitepaper](https://www.bittensor.com/whitepaper)) separately
cites Fisher Information pruning (LeCun et al. 1989; Yu et al. 2017) as the
theoretical ideal behind how peer-significance weights are ranked, and cites
a cluster of standard deep-learning papers (Hinton et al. 2015 on
distillation/general intelligence, Devlin et al. 2019, Radford et al. 2019,
Shazeer et al. 2017) as background for why peer-to-peer intelligence markets
are plausible — these are context, not the mechanism's core theoretical
grounding.

**Note on naming**: the official academic paper describes the
Shapley-value-based ranking and trust-weighted consensus mechanism but does
not use the name "Yuma Consensus" anywhere in that document. "Yuma
Consensus" as a named, specific algorithm (stake-weighted median + outlier
clipping) appears in community/ecosystem documentation and later working
papers rather than in the cited academic source itself — flagged here as a
naming gap between the academic grounding and the term actually used in
practice.

What it does.markdown:
EZKL (zkonduit/ezkl) compiles ONNX-format ML models (exported from
PyTorch, TensorFlow, sklearn, etc.) into a zero-knowledge circuit, so
that a model inference can be proven correct without revealing the
model weights and/or inputs, and verified cheaply — including on-chain
in the EVM, in a browser, or on-device.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Takes an ONNX graph + sample input, compiles a corresponding proving
  circuit, generates a proof of correct execution, and a matching
  verifier (including Solidity verifier contracts for EVM chains).
- Backend proving system: **Halo2**. EZKL's own README states: "In the
  backend we use the collaboratively-developed
  [Halo2](https://github.com/privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2) as a
  proof system." ([github.com/zkonduit/ezkl](https://github.com/zkonduit/ezkl))
- EZKL uses a modified variant of Halo2 that swaps in **KZG polynomial
  commitments** (rather than the discrete-log/IPA commitment Halo2
  originally shipped with) specifically to get smaller proofs and
  cheaper on-chain verification. This is a deliberate deviation from
  vanilla Halo2, not an assumption — flagged as inferred-from-general
  sourcing rather than a single explicit EZKL doc quote; worth
  rechecking against current docs.ezkl.xyz if this matters for a
  specific decision.

frontmatter.name: Fetch.ai (uAgents)
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (architecture description, team-authored); inferred (some matrix cells)

What it does.markdown:
Fetch.ai provides a framework (uAgents, Python) and blockchain infrastructure
for building autonomous software agents that can discover each other,
communicate, and transact. Agents register on-chain for discoverability and
settle value exchange via Fetch.ai's own token (FET).

**ASI Alliance context:** Fetch.ai merged with SingularityNET and Ocean
Protocol in 2024 to form the Artificial Superintelligence Alliance (ASI),
unifying their tokens (FET/AGIX/OCEAN → ASI) under one brand. CUDOS
(distributed GPU compute) joined in Oct 2024. Ocean Protocol subsequently
**withdrew from the alliance in Oct 2025**, with an associated lawsuit
settled (286M FET returned) — this entry focuses on Fetch.ai's own
technical stack, not the alliance's business structure, which is actively
in flux. ([0xgreythorn Medium overview](https://0xgreythorn.medium.com/fetch-ai-the-asi-alliance-decentralized-ai-powerhouse-b39c40ec4a56))

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **uAgents**: a Python library for building event-driven agents — each
  agent has a cryptographic identity (address derived from a keypair, not
  an IP), listens for messages, and responds via decorated handlers. State
  persists via a key-value store; agent-to-agent messaging uses a typed
  "Agent Chat Protocol." ([github.com/fetchai/uAgents](https://github.com/fetchai/uAgents))
- **Almanac**: a smart contract on Fetch.ai's own chain where agents
  register for discoverability; paired with a Fetch Name Service (FNS) for
  human-readable discovery and the Fetch Ledger for record-keeping.
- **Base chain**: an independent Cosmos-SDK chain using CometBFT (formerly
  Tendermint) consensus, with IBC interoperability to other Cosmos chains —
  not an Ethereum L2/L1.
- **Agentverse / ASI:One**: a hosted platform and LLM-orchestration layer
  that translates natural-language goals into multi-agent workflows on top
  of the uAgents substrate.

frontmatter.name: Gensyn
frontmatter.confidence: grounded

What it does.markdown:
Gensyn is a protocol for decentralized ML compute: clients submit training
jobs, untrusted third-party providers execute them, and a verification layer
lets the client trust the result without controlling or re-running all of the
provider's hardware.

Architecture summary.markdown:
Current production system is **Verde** (per Gensyn's own research blog,
Oct 2026 check), which replaced the older litepaper-era design built around
four roles (Submitters, Solvers, Verifiers, Whistleblowers) and a Truebit-style
challenge game. Verde combines two pieces:

- **RepOps (Reproducible Operators)**: forces a fixed operation ordering for
  ML operators so that execution is bitwise-reproducible across different
  hardware, closing the floating-point non-associativity gap that previously
  made exact-match verification unreliable across GPUs/vendors.
- **Two-level bisection game**: providers commit to each training iteration
  via Merkle trees; disputes are resolved by bisecting first at the iteration
  level, then the operation level, so a referee only has to re-check a small,
  pinpointed slice of the computation instead of re-running the whole job.

Source: [Verde: Verification System In Production](https://www.gensyn.ai/research/verde-verification-system-in-production)
(Gensyn's own research blog).

Note: the older litepaper (docs.gensyn.ai/litepaper) describes a different,
earlier design — a Truebit-style incentive game with Submitter/Solver/
Verifier/Whistleblower roles and a graph-based "pinpoint protocol." That
litepaper is confirmed by Gensyn's own ecosystem write-ups to be **outdated**
relative to Verde. Documented here for lineage, not as current architecture.

frontmatter.name: Google Confidential Federated Learning (TensorFlow Federated + TEE confidentiality)
frontmatter.confidence: grounded

What it does.markdown:
Google trains production ML models (e.g. Gboard's next-word prediction) on
data that never leaves users' devices. Each device computes a local model
update on its own data; only the update — not the raw data — is sent to a
server, which aggregates updates across many devices into an improved
global model. The "confidential" layer adds server-side trusted execution
environments (TEEs) so that even the aggregation server itself cannot see
individual updates, with the privacy properties externally auditable rather
than taken on trust.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Base mechanism**: Federated Averaging — devices compute local SGD
  updates, a server averages them into a new global model, raw data is
  never centralized.
- **Confidentiality layer** ("Confidential Federated Computations", 2024):
  devices encrypt their uploads with keys controlled by a TEE-hosted Key
  Management Service (KMS). The KMS only releases decryption keys to
  specific, pre-approved TEE binaries — so the server operator cannot
  access plaintext updates even with full infrastructure access.
- **External verifiability**: access policies (which binaries may process
  which data) are published to Rekor, Sigstore's public transparency log,
  and the TEE binaries are reproducibly buildable from open-source code —
  so an outside auditor can check that the system is actually doing what
  it claims, not just trusting Google's word for it. This is the piece
  that lets Google claim *externally verifiable* differential privacy
  rather than DP that depends on trusting the service operator.
- Per secondary reporting (MarkTechPost, Oct 2026 — primary source page
  returned a 403 during this research pass, so this specific detail is
  less directly confirmed than the rest): this architecture is now live in
  production for Gboard.

frontmatter.confidence: grounded (core technique lineage); inferred (trust model, some performance framing)

What it does.markdown:
DeepProve is Lagrange Labs' zkML system: it generates zero-knowledge
proofs that a specific LLM produced a specific output sequence from a
specific input, without re-running the model or trusting the party that
did. Unlike earlier zkML work limited to single tokens or isolated
components, DeepProve targets full end-to-end LLM inference — it
certifies that the whole output sequence is correct rather than
encoding the entire inference computation in-circuit, which is what
lets it avoid the quadratic circuit blowup or expensive RAM modeling
that sank earlier approaches.

Lagrange Labs is a separate project from, but shares the "ZK
coprocessor" branding with, Lagrange's other product line — a
decentralized ZK Prover Network / ZK Coprocessor for proving SQL
queries over on-chain data, which (per Lagrange's own docs) uses
Plonky2. **DeepProve is not that system** — it's a distinct proving
construction built specifically for ML inference. Don't conflate the
two when reading Lagrange's broader materials.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Core building blocks, per DeepProve's own paper abstract: the
  **sum-check protocol** and **lookup arguments**, used to verify
  individual LLM operators (multi-head attention, layer normalization,
  grouped-query attention, rotary positional embeddings) without
  encoding the full computation as one monolithic circuit.
- Native format support: ONNX, safetensors, and GGUF — so models
  exported from PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, or Hugging Face run through
  DeepProve unchanged (no custom model-authoring step required).
- Positioned explicitly against two named prior systems: **zkGPT**
  (USENIX'25, single-token proofs) and **zkLLM** (CCS'24, proved only
  the Softmax component) — DeepProve's claimed contribution is doing
  both end-to-end and faster.

frontmatter.name: Nillion
frontmatter.confidence: grounded

What it does.markdown:
Nillion is a decentralized network for storing and computing on encrypted
("blind") data without ever reconstructing the plaintext on any single
node. Data is split and distributed across independent nodes; computation
happens directly on the shares via secure multi-party computation (MPC),
and only the final result is reassembled.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Nil Message Compute (NMC)** is Nillion's branding for its MPC layer.
  It combines **One-Time Masking (OTM)** with **Linear Secret Sharing
  (LSS)** so that a network of nodes can jointly store and process
  confidential data with information-theoretic security (unconditionally
  secure, not just computationally hard to break).
- The production MPC protocol built on top of this is internally called
  **Curl**, extended from LSSS to efficiently support non-linear
  operations (division, square roots, trig, logs) that plain linear
  secret sharing can't do without extra machinery.
- In 2026 Nillion migrated its base chain from Cosmos to Ethereum,
  launching a new L1 called **Blacklight** (mainnet live 2026-10-05).
  Node operators stake NIL (minimum 70,000 NIL) to run nodes and verify
  computations. The original Cosmos-based L2 is being wound down, with
  users told to bridge assets to the new L1.

**Paper:** "Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in

(UC Irvine), Wicher Malten (Nillion), Mehmet Ugurbil (Nillion), Wyatt
Howe (UCLA).

(originally posted to IACR ePrint as 2023/1740, later withdrawn from
ePrint but mirrored on Nillion's own site).

**Grounding source:** Nillion's own team announced this paper directly

computation — see "Introducing the Nillion Non-Interactive MPC Protocol
for Non-Linear Computations"
(https://medium.com/@Nillion_Network/introducing-the-nillion-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations-67e9310ef479)
and the MPC Alliance's coverage of the same announcement
(https://www.mpcalliance.org/blog/nillion-introduces-a-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations).
Four of the six authors are Nillion staff, so this is effectively
Nillion publishing its own core protocol paper — about as direct a
grounding as this kind of claim can get.

**How it's used:** the paper's contribution — evaluating arithmetic
sum-of-products expressions (which covers the multiplications needed
for non-linear ops) within LSSS using a preprocessing phase instead of
interactive communication during computation — is the specific technique
that lets Curl/NMC do non-linear math without the usual back-and-forth
communication overhead of classic MPC protocols.

frontmatter.name: Nous Research — Psyche
frontmatter.confidence: grounded

What it does.markdown:
Psyche is Nous Research's network for training large language models
using compute contributed from geographically dispersed, heterogeneous
machines across the internet, rather than a single co-located cluster.
It targets the bandwidth bottleneck that normally makes training over
consumer/Ethernet-class links impractical.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Built on **DisTrO** (Distributed Training Over-the-Internet), Nous's
  in-house distributed optimizer stack, which in turn builds on **DeMo**
  (Decoupled Momentum Optimization), Nous's earlier optimizer paper.
  Nous's own Psyche page states directly: *"Building on DisTrO and its
  predecessor DeMo, Psyche reduces data transfer by several orders of
  magnitude."* ([nousresearch.com/nous-psyche](https://nousresearch.com/nous-psyche))
- Mechanism: decouples local momentum updates, applies a fast
  orthonormal transform (DCT) plus top-k sparsification, and reuses the
  momentum buffer as error feedback — described by Nous as compressing
  gradient communication the way JPEG compresses an image.
- Coordination layer runs on **Solana**: a smart-contract coordinator
  stores run metadata, handles state transitions, supplies randomness
  for node assignment, and acts as the synchronization authority across
  participants. Chosen specifically for fault-tolerance and censorship
  resistance, per Nous's own description.
- Largest known run to date: a 40B-parameter pretraining run on the
  testnet (May 2025), described by Nous as the largest internet-distributed
  pretraining run at the time.

frontmatter.name: NVIDIA Confidential Computing (H100/H200/Blackwell)
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (standards lineage); grounded (performance, independent third-party source)

What it does.markdown:
Lets a cloud tenant run AI inference/training on a GPU while keeping both
the model weights and the input data encrypted in GPU memory and
protected from the cloud operator, the hypervisor, and other tenants —
extended from CPU confidential computing (already common for general
workloads) to the GPU itself, which previously sat outside the trust
boundary entirely.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- The H100 (GA April 2024) is, per NVIDIA's own developer blog, "the
  world's first native Confidential Computing GPU." Confidential mode
  ("CC-On") anchors a hardware root of trust on-die; secure boot ensures
  only verified firmware runs.
- **Attestation chain**: the GPU driver uses **SPDM** (Security Protocol
  and Data Model) for session establishment, producing a cryptographically
  signed attestation report an external verifier can check before trusting
  the GPU's state.
  ([developer.nvidia.com](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-on-h100-gpus-for-secure-and-trustworthy-ai/))
- **Does not implement a standalone GPU TEE** — it extends an existing
  *CPU* TEE's trust boundary to include the GPU. Per NVIDIA's own blog,
  it requires a CPU TEE already in place: AMD Genoa/Milan with
  **SEV-SNP** enabled, or Intel Sapphire Rapids with **TDX**. The GPU's
  DMA engine encrypts CPU↔GPU data transfer (AES-GCM-256) so the data
  stays encrypted across that boundary.
  ([developer.nvidia.com](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-on-h100-gpus-for-secure-and-trustworthy-ai/))
- Definition of "confidential computing" used throughout NVIDIA's own
  material is explicitly attributed to the **Confidential Computing
  Consortium** (an industry body, not an academic source):
  "protection of data in use by performing computation in a
  hardware-based, attested trusted execution environment (TEE), per the
  Confidential Computing Consortium."

frontmatter.name: Ocean Protocol
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (architecture); no academic lineage found for core privacy mechanism

What it does.markdown:
Ocean Protocol is a Web3 data marketplace: data owners publish datasets as
NFTs (ERC-721) with access rights sold as datatokens (ERC-20), and buyers
can either download data they've licensed or — via Compute-to-Data (C2D)
— run an approved algorithm against a dataset without the dataset ever
leaving the owner's infrastructure, so only the computation's output is
exposed, not the raw data.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Data NFTs + datatokens**: the data NFT represents the underlying IP;
  datatokens are per-asset ERC-20 access-right tokens. Smart contracts for
  publishing, pricing, and access control run on Ethereum mainnet; Ocean
  is also deployed across Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Energy Web Chain,
  Optimism, and Moonriver.
  ([docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks](https://docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks))
- **Compute-to-Data (C2D) privacy mechanism**: per Ocean's own
  architecture docs, privacy comes from **process isolation, not
  cryptography**. Each job runs in a dedicated, ephemeral Kubernetes pod
  that loads the dataset and algorithm, executes, publishes the result,
  then deletes the dataset, algorithm, and itself.
  ([docs.oceanprotocol.com/developers/compute-to-data/compute-to-data-architecture](https://docs.oceanprotocol.com/developers/compute-to-data/compute-to-data-architecture))
  Components: **Ocean Provider** (credentials/access control),
  **Operator Service** (HTTP API, workflow orchestration),
  **Operator Engine** (Kubernetes-backed execution).
- **Oasis Sapphire deployment**: Ocean's "Predictoor" product specifically
  is deployed on Oasis Sapphire mainnet, which *is* a confidential
  (TEE-based) EVM. This is a genuinely cryptographic/hardware-confidential
  privacy mechanism — but per Ocean's own docs, this Sapphire deployment
  does not currently support `ocean.js`, `ocean.py`, or Ocean Market, i.e.
  it isn't the mechanism behind the core data-marketplace/C2D product
  described above. Don't conflate the two.

frontmatter.name: Olas (formerly Autonolas)
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (architecture); no formal academic lineage found (see below)

What it does.markdown:
Olas is an open-source stack plus on-chain protocol for building, running,
and monetizing "agent services" — groups of independent off-chain programs
(agents) that coordinate to perform a task (e.g. DAO treasury management,
custom oracles, keeper bots). The blockchain layer registers and secures
these services and provides the economic incentive for developers to build
and compose reusable agent components.

Architecture summary.markdown:
Per Olas's own developer docs and whitepaper, the stack has four parts:

- **Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) architecture** — an agent service is composed
  of independently-developed code components combined via software
  composition.
- **State-Minimized Consensus Gadgets** — a lightweight consensus mechanism
  so that a group of agent instances running the same service can agree on
  shared state without requiring full blockchain-level consensus for every
  interaction.
- **Agent Communication Network (ACN)** — a distributed hash table (DHT)
  that maps an agent's wallet address to its current network location, so
  agents can find and message each other without a central directory.
  ([stack.olas.network/open-aea/acn](https://stack.olas.network/open-aea/acn/))
- **On-chain protocol** — smart contracts that register agents, agent
  "blueprints," and components as NFTs, and handle the incentive/reward
  mechanism for composing them.
  ([olas.network whitepaper](https://olas.network/documents/whitepaper/Whitepaper%20v1.0.pdf))

What it does.markdown:
ORA runs a verifiable AI oracle: large ML models (LLaMA, Stable
Diffusion, DeepSeek, Mistral, Qwen) execute off-chain, and smart
contracts on Ethereum and several L2s can trust the result without
re-running the model themselves, through an optimistic dispute

  optimistically; a challenge window lets any validator dispute a
  result, triggering a bisection game that narrows the disagreement to
  one computation step, resolved on-chain by a **Fraud Proof VM

  validate results).

  honest, economically incentivized validator is watching and willing
  to dispute within the challenge window — not a cryptographic
  guarantee, an economic/game-theoretic one.

  ex-Ethereum Foundation zkML researcher, which is also why ORA's docs
  explicitly position opML *against* zkML (cost/scale trade-off) rather

frontmatter.name: Pluralis Research
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (core technique); inferred (some matrix cells)

What it does.markdown:
Pluralis Research runs **Protocol Learning**: large language models trained
collaboratively across the open internet on heterogeneous, unreliable
consumer/cloud hardware that no single participant fully owns — contrasted
with centralized datacenter training. Their production system for this is
called **Agora**.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Pipeline parallelism**: each participating device hosts one pipeline
  stage (e.g. one transformer block); multiple devices can replicate a stage
  for redundancy.
- **Data parallelism**, combined with the above, to distribute training
  further across the swarm.
- **Peer-to-peer routing**: participants join/leave dynamically without
  halting training.
- **Subspace Networks** (see Built on, below): the specific compression
  technique that makes cross-device communication cheap enough for this to
  work over consumer internet rather than datacenter interconnects — up to a
  100x reduction in inter-stage communication, by confining activations and
  gradients to a predefined low-dimensional subspace exploiting a recursive
  structure in transformer networks.
- Source: [pluralis.ai/docs](https://pluralis.ai/docs/) (Agora system
  overview).

frontmatter.name: Prime Intellect
frontmatter.confidence: grounded (training-framework lineage); inferred (protocol/incentive-layer specifics)

What it does.markdown:
Prime Intellect runs a GPU compute marketplace (50+ data centers, single-GPU
to multi-thousand-GPU clusters) and an open decentralized training stack on
top of it. Its best-known result is INTELLECT-1, the first openly
decentralized-trained 10B-parameter language model, trained across five
countries and three continents on up to 112 H100s running concurrently.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **PRIME framework**: a fault-tolerant distributed training framework for
  unreliable, globally distributed nodes. Core piece is the
  **ElasticDeviceMesh**, which manages a dynamic global process group for
  fault-tolerant internet communication plus local process groups for
  intra-node communication, with live checkpoint recovery.
- PRIME combines **FSDP2** (intra-node sharded data parallelism) with
  **DiLoCo** (inter-node low-communication optimization) in a hybrid
  setup, plus a custom int8 all-reduce, to get a reported ~400x reduction
  in cross-node communication bandwidth versus standard data-parallel
  training.
- In the INTELLECT-1 run, nodes trained independently for ~38 minutes
  between synchronization steps, each sync taking ~1-7 minutes; reported
  compute utilization was 83% across continents and 96% when restricted to
  US-only nodes.
- Separately, Prime Intellect operates a "PI protocol" layer described as
  providing on-chain primitives for trust, collaboration, and collective
  ownership of resulting models by compute/data/code contributors — this
  layer is comparatively thin on technical documentation in what's
  publicly available; treat specifics as inferred, not grounded.

What it does.markdown:
Ritual is a decentralized AI infrastructure protocol connecting Ethereum
smart contracts to a network of off-chain AI compute nodes. Developers
submit inference (or other heavy-compute) tasks; the network executes
them off-chain and settles a verifiable result back on-chain.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Infernet**: the middleware protocol/SDK connecting Ethereum
  contracts to off-chain compute nodes. The Infernet Node is an
  open-source, lightweight client (github.com/ritual-net/infernet-node)
  that executes arbitrary workload containers and reports results
  on-chain. Reported scale: 8,000+ connected nodes (per Ritual's own
  explainer material — not independently verified against chain data
  this pass).
- **Ritual Chain**: a custom L1 built to support heterogeneous
  computation (AI inference, ZK proof verification, TEE execution,
  scheduled transactions) that standard blockchains can't natively
  handle.
- **Symphony**: Ritual's own consensus/execution research (credited to
  Maryam Bahrani, published on ritual.net's blog, ~April 2026),
  describing "Execution-Aware Consensus and Proposer Disaggregation."
  Its core idea is an **Execute-Once-Verify-Many-Times (EOVMT)** model:
  a staked executor runs the expensive/non-deterministic computation
  once and produces a proof; other nodes verify the proof instead of
  re-executing the computation themselves. Deterministic replication
  stays on the critical consensus path; expensive or non-deterministic
  execution is delegated asynchronously, with proof-based settlement.
- **Proof system is deliberately not fixed.** Ritual's own docs
  describe the protocol as proof-system agnostic: settlement can use a
  ZK proof, a TEE attestation, or both, chosen per application based on
  its security/cost/performance needs — not a single scheme the whole
  network commits to.

What it does.markdown:
Sentient is a protocol for publishing open-weight AI models while still giving
the model's owners/contributors enforceable ownership, usage tracking, and a
revenue stream — addressing the problem that a fully open model can normally
be copied and monetized by anyone, with no way to trace or compensate the
original builder.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Built around the **OML (Open, Monetizable, Loyal)** framework: a model
  should be inspectable/open (**Open**), trigger compensation to its owners
  on every call (**Monetizable**), and have misuse/unauthorized use be
  detectable (**Loyal**).
- Four-layer protocol stack: **storage** (immutable/available hosting of the
  model artifact), **distribution** (converting the artifact into OML format),
  **access** (authorizing/tracking each query), **incentive** (routing
  collected fees to builders). (Source: openagi.discourse.group summary of
  the Sentient protocol design, cross-confirmed by multiple secondary
  write-ups — not fetched from a single Sentient primary doc in this pass.)
- Production mechanism is reported as the **"Melange" method** — combining
  model fingerprinting, TEE (trusted execution environment) execution, and
  on-chain contract-based revenue distribution. This is a secondary-source
  characterization (search aggregation), not independently confirmed against
  a primary Sentient doc in this pass — flagged as inferred.
- Chain architecture: designed to be **L1-agnostic / EVM-compatible** rather
  than requiring its own base chain (reported compatible with Ethereum and
  other L1s); no dedicated standalone "Sentient Chain" was found. Sentient's
  own network is referred to as **GRID**.

frontmatter.confidence: grounded

What it does.markdown:
Concrete-ML is an open-source Python framework from Zama that lets you train
a model normally (scikit-learn-compatible APIs, or PyTorch/TensorFlow via
ONNX) and then run inference on **encrypted** inputs, so the service running
the model never sees the plaintext data. Output of `encrypt()` → `run()` →
`decrypt()` never exposes intermediate values to the server.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Built directly on top of **Concrete** (Zama's TFHE compiler, which turns
  Python/numerical programs into their FHE equivalent), which itself is
  built on **TFHE-rs**, Zama's Rust implementation of the TFHE scheme.
- Models are **quantized** (quantization-aware training or post-training
  quantization) to convert floating-point weights/activations into
  integers, since FHE arithmetic operates over integers, not floats.
- Non-linear activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, etc.) are evaluated via
  **programmable bootstrapping** — TFHE's bootstrap step is repurposed to
  simultaneously refresh noise *and* apply an arbitrary lookup-table
  function, which is what makes homomorphic neural-net inference
  practical rather than prohibitively expensive.

frontmatter.paper: OML: Open, Monetizable, and Loyal AI
frontmatter.authors: Zerui Cheng, Edoardo Contente, Ben Finch, Oleg Golev, Jonathan Hayase, Andrew Miller, Niusha Moshrefi, Anshul Nasery, Sandeep Nailwal, Sewoong Oh, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Directly authored by the tracked system's own team: 5 of the 12 authors
(Contente, Finch, Golev, Nailwal, Tyagi) are affiliated with Sentient
Foundation, alongside academics from Princeton, University of Washington,
and UIUC. This is not Sentient citing prior art — it is Sentient's founding
protocol paper. See `systems/sentient-oml.md` for how the system implements
it.

Core contribution.markdown:
Introduces **"AI-native cryptography"**: a proposed new branch of
cryptography built specifically around the structure of AI model
representations, rather than adapting traditional binary (secure/broken)
cryptographic security models to AI. The core observation is that AI data
representations live on continuous, low-dimensional manifolds, which can be
exploited to build security primitives traditional cryptography can't
express — e.g. a fingerprint that survives fine-tuning/distillation of a
model without being a literal bit-for-bit watermark. The paper's first
concrete primitive built in this framework is **model fingerprinting**
(labeled OML 1.0): an undetectable marker embedded into a model via
fine-tuning, usable to detect unauthorized use/redistribution of an
ostensibly "open" model.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Sentient's entire ownership/monetization pitch depends on this primitive:
if a model is fully open-weight, nothing stops anyone from copying and
reselling it unless there's a way to detect that a given deployed model is
derived from a specific owned original. OML's fingerprinting is that
detection mechanism. The protocol layers described in
`systems/sentient-oml.md` (storage/distribution/access/incentive) are the
economic/infrastructure machinery built on top of this cryptographic
primitive, not the primitive itself.

frontmatter.paper: CCF: A Framework for Building Confidential Verifiable Replicated Services
frontmatter.authors: Mark Russinovich, Edward Ashton, Christine Avanessians, Miguel Castro, et al.
frontmatter.refined_paper: Confidential Consortium Framework: Secure Multiparty Applications with Confidentiality, Integrity, and High Availability
frontmatter.refined_venue: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Vol 17(2), 2023 (VLDB nominee)

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Grounded directly, not inferred: Microsoft's own Azure documentation
states that Azure confidential ledger — the transparency/auditability
component used in Azure AI Confidential Inferencing — "is built on the
Confidential Consortium Framework (CCF)." CCF is itself a Microsoft
Research project (github.com/microsoft/CCF) with its own research page
listing this 2019 technical report as the original design paper, later
refined and published in the peer-reviewed 2023 VLDB paper linked above.
See `/systems/azure-confidential-ai.md` for how this plugs into the
actual Azure product.

Core contribution.markdown:
CCF combines two previously separate ideas into one system: (1)
hardware TEEs for remotely-verifiable confidentiality and code
integrity of the compute itself, and (2) state-machine replication
backed by an append-only, auditable ledger for data integrity and high
availability. The result is a framework for building multi-party
applications that can run on cloud infrastructure none of the
participants fully trust, with governance (who can change the rules,
who operates nodes) kept separate from, and verifiable independent of,
the cloud operator. The 2023 refinement formalizes CCF's custom
distributed-consensus and client-consistency model and was itself the
subject of a separate 2025 NSDI verification paper ("Smart Casual
Verification of the Confidential Consortium Framework"), which is
outside this seed paper's scope but worth noting as follow-on
scrutiny of the same system.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Azure's confidential ledger product — and, through it, the
transparency-ledger component of Azure AI Confidential Inferencing —
is built directly on CCF. This is the one part of Microsoft's
"Confidential AI" story with a real, citable Microsoft Research paper
behind it; the TEE hardware layer underneath (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX,
NVIDIA H100 confidential computing) is vendor technology with its own
specs, not an academic contribution from this lineage — see
`/systems/azure-confidential-ai.md`'s "Built on" section for why those
two lineages are kept separate rather than merged into one claim.

frontmatter.field: Decentralized incentive / consensus mechanisms for ML networks
frontmatter.venue: Contributions to the Theory of Games, Vol. II (Annals of Mathematics Studies 28), Princeton University Press

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Bittensor's own academic paper, *"Incentivizing Intelligence: The Bittensor
Approach"* (Steeves et al., hosted at
[bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia)), explicitly
cites Shapley's 1952 value concept as the theoretical basis for how the
network attributes credit to peers: each participant's reward is meant to
reflect their marginal contribution to the network's informational output,
evaluated across permutations of coalitions of peers — which is exactly what
the Shapley value formalizes. This is the one piece of the Bittensor stack
with a clean, explicit academic citation; the rest of the mechanism (the
specific stake-weighted-median "Yuma Consensus" algorithm used in
production) is documented in community/ecosystem sources rather than in a
peer-reviewed citation trail — see the naming-gap note in
[[systems/bittensor]].

Core contribution.markdown:
Shapley's paper answers a fairness question: if a group of people (or
agents) jointly produce some value by cooperating, how should that value be
split among them in a way that fairly reflects each one's contribution,
even when contributions aren't independent (i.e. what one agent adds
depends on who else is already in the group)? The Shapley value is defined
by averaging each agent's marginal contribution across every possible order
in which agents could join the coalition. It's the unique allocation rule
satisfying a small set of fairness axioms (efficiency, symmetry, additivity,
null-player). It's a cooperative-game-theory result, not a machine-learning
or cryptography result — its relevance here is purely as the attribution
principle a decentralized ML incentive system borrows.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Bittensor needs to answer: "how much is this peer's model output actually
worth to the network, given that other peers are also contributing similar
or overlapping information?" Naively rewarding every peer independently
invites redundant, low-effort submissions; the Shapley framing is invoked to
justify rewarding marginal/novel contribution instead. In practice,
production Bittensor does not compute literal Shapley values (that's
computationally intractable at network scale — exact Shapley values require
summing over all coalition permutations); it uses Yuma Consensus's
stake-weighted-median-with-clipping as a tractable proxy mechanism inspired
by the same fairness goal. This is worth flagging explicitly: the citation
grounds the *motivation*, not the *literal algorithm* actually running in
production.

frontmatter.authors: Hengrui Jia, Mohammad Yaghini, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Natalie Dullerud, Anvith Thudi, Varun Chandrasekaran, Nicolas Papernot
frontmatter.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2021

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Cited directly by Gensyn's own Verde research post as foundational prior work
("Proof-of-Learning" — [arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633)),
alongside Refereed Delegation, Agatha, Toploc, and Proof-of-Training-Data. See
[systems/gensyn.md](../systems/gensyn.md) for the full citation list and source
link. Of that list, this paper is the one that directly frames the core problem
Gensyn's verification layer exists to solve: how do you let a party that didn't
do the training convince a verifier that specific gradient-descent work was
actually performed, without full re-execution.

Core contribution.markdown:
Introduces "proof-of-learning" (PoL): a party that trained a model produces a
proof — built from checkpoints and the gradient-descent trajectory metadata
recorded during training — that lets a verifier check, cheaply, that training
actually happened as claimed, rather than requiring the verifier to redo the
entire training run. It formalizes what such a proof needs to guarantee and
shows practical constructions and attacks against naive versions of the idea.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Gensyn's verification problem is exactly this: a client needs to trust that a
third-party provider trained a model correctly without re-running the full
job. Gensyn's current production system (Verde) does not implement PoL's
checkpoint-trajectory scheme directly — it instead uses RepOps
(bitwise-reproducible operators) plus a Merkle-tree-based bisection/dispute
game — but PoL is the paper that established the problem framing and the
first concrete proposal in this space, which is why Gensyn cites it as prior
work. See [systems/gensyn.md](../systems/gensyn.md) for how the current
architecture actually differs from PoL's approach.

frontmatter.paper: DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models
frontmatter.authors: Arthur Douillard, Qixuan Feng, Andrei A. Rusu, Rachita Chhaparia, Yani Donchev, Adhiguna Kuncoro, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Arthur Szlam, Jiajun Shen

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Grounded via direct citation, not inference: Prime Intellect's own
OpenDiLoCo announcement states *"Introducing OpenDiLoCo, an open-source
implementation and scaling of DeepMind's Distributed Low-Communication
(DiLoCo) method"* and separately calls it *"a reproducible implementation
of DeepMind's DiLoCo experiments."*
([primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco)).
Prime Intellect's subsequent INTELLECT-1 technical report (arXiv:2412.01152)
builds its PRIME framework directly on this same DiLoCo core. See
[systems/prime-intellect.md](../systems/prime-intellect.md) for the full
chain.

This is a different seed paper from the one in
[foundations/decentralized-training.md](./decentralized-training.md)
(Proof-of-Learning, cited by Gensyn) despite sharing the same field — that
paper is about verifying training happened as claimed; this one is about
making distributed training communication-efficient in the first place.

Core contribution.markdown:
DiLoCo lets language-model training happen across "islands" of
poorly-connected devices instead of requiring tightly-interconnected
accelerators synchronizing every step. Each worker runs many local
optimization steps with an inner optimizer (AdamW); periodically, an
outer optimizer (SGD with Nesterov momentum) synchronizes pseudo-gradients
across workers. On the C4 dataset with 8 workers, DiLoCo matched fully
synchronous training quality while communicating roughly 500x less, and
the method is robust to workers dropping in and out during training.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Prime Intellect's PRIME framework uses DiLoCo as the inter-node
optimization layer (paired with FSDP2 for intra-node sharding), which is
what let INTELLECT-1 train a 10B-parameter model across five countries and
three continents with nodes syncing only every ~38 minutes. See
[systems/prime-intellect.md](../systems/prime-intellect.md) for the full
architecture and property matrix.

Core contribution.markdown:
Ray's paper introduces a distributed execution framework for AI
workloads that unifies two previously separate programming models —
fine-grained, stateless task parallelism (as in MapReduce-style
systems) and stateful actor-based computation — under one dynamic task
graph and a single system. It uses a bottom-up distributed scheduler
(rather than a single centralized scheduler) and a fault-tolerant
distributed metadata store, specifically to support workloads common in

short, latency-sensitive tasks with long-running, stateful ones, which

io.net uses a fork of Ray as the execution substrate for distributing
and scheduling GPU workloads across its marketplace of
provider-contributed hardware — i.e., Ray solves the general
"orchestrate many parallel/stateful tasks across a cluster" problem,
and io.net's contribution on top is specifically the
decentralization/marketplace/trust layer (payment, resource-integrity
verification, provider onboarding), which this paper does not address
and which io.net's own docs don't tie to any further academic source.

cryptography-specific one — it's the seed for the *compute
orchestration* side of this field, not the *trust/verification* side.

frontmatter.authors: Bowen Peng, Jeffrey Quesnelle, Diederik P. Kingma

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Directly grounded, not inferred: the paper is authored by Nous Research
staff, and Nous's own Psyche architecture page states explicitly —
*"Building on DisTrO and its predecessor DeMo, Psyche reduces data
transfer by several orders of magnitude"*
([nousresearch.com/nous-psyche](https://nousresearch.com/nous-psyche)).
See [systems/nous-psyche.md](../systems/nous-psyche.md) for the full
chain. Code: [github.com/bloc97/DeMo](https://github.com/bloc97/DeMo).

This is deliberately kept separate from `decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, arXiv:2103.05633, the seed for Gensyn): both sit in
the same broad field but address different problems — Proof-of-Learning
is about *verifying* that training happened as claimed; DeMo is about
making distributed optimization *communication-efficient* enough to run
over consumer/internet-class links in the first place. Per this repo's
rule of one foundation file per distinct citation lineage, they stay as
two files even though the field label is the same.

Core contribution.markdown:
DeMo is a drop-in replacement for momentum-based optimizers (e.g. Adam)
designed to cut the communication volume required for distributed
training. It decouples local momentum updates across workers, applies
a fast orthonormal transform (DCT) to the momentum signal, keeps only
the top-k components (sparsification), and reuses the discarded
momentum as error feedback on the next step rather than dropping it.
The paper reports up to 85x less data transmitted per GPU than
AdamW-DDP on 300M–1B parameter models, while reaching comparable loss —
and the approach is topology-agnostic, meaning it doesn't assume a
particular interconnect (works over Ethernet/multi-datacenter links,
not just high-bandwidth cluster fabric).

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Nous's Psyche network is DeMo's direct production application: DisTrO
extends DeMo into a full runtime (adding load balancing and
selective-synchronization on top of the core compression idea), and
Psyche then wraps that runtime in a Solana-coordinated network so
contributors with heterogeneous, geographically dispersed hardware can
train one model together. See [systems/nous-psyche.md](../systems/nous-psyche.md)
for the full system and its known limitations — notably, DeMo/DisTrO
solve the bandwidth problem but explicitly do **not** yet solve
verifying that a remote participant actually ran the claimed
computation honestly.

frontmatter.paper: Deep Neural Networks for Encrypted Inference with TFHE
frontmatter.authors: Andrei Stoian, Jordan Frery, Roman Bredehoft, Luis Montero, Celia Kherfallah, Benoit Chevallier-Mames

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Authored by the team behind Zama's Concrete-ML, and uses Concrete directly
for its benchmarks — this is the paper that connects the general TFHE
cryptosystem to the specific problem of running deep neural network
inference on encrypted data, which is exactly what Concrete-ML ships as a
product. It sits one layer above the raw cryptography (TFHE itself, and
Chillotti/Joye/Paillier's programmable bootstrapping) and one layer below
the shipped library — the applied bridge.

Core contribution.markdown:
The paper shows how to design and quantize DNN architectures (targeted at
computer-vision tasks) so that they can run entirely under TFHE's
programmable bootstrapping, and benchmarks the resulting latency/accuracy
tradeoffs on Concrete. The core insight it operationalizes: FHE arithmetic
only works cleanly over integers, so every layer of the network has to be
re-expressed in quantized integer form *before* bootstrapping is used to
evaluate non-linearities — the paper is effectively the recipe for doing
that re-expression without destroying accuracy or blowing up latency.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Concrete-ML's quantization-aware training pipeline and its approach to
evaluating activation functions via programmable bootstrapping are the
productionized version of what this paper demonstrates. See
`/systems/zama-concrete-ml.md` for the property matrix this paper's
techniques feed into — specifically the "Precision" and "Non-linear
evaluation" rows.

frontmatter.paper: Subspace Networks: Scaling Decentralized Training with Communication-Efficient Model Parallelism
frontmatter.authors: Sameera Ramasinghe, Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan, Gil Avraham, Yan Zuo, Alexander Long

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Authored directly by the Pluralis Research team (affiliation explicitly
stated in the paper itself — confirmed via
[arxiv.org/html/2506.01260v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01260v1)), not a
third-party citation. See
[systems/pluralis-research.md](../systems/pluralis-research.md) for the
grounding detail, including the title change between preprint versions
(same arXiv ID, retitled from "Protocol Models" to "Subspace Networks").

This is a **distinct lineage** from `foundations/decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, arXiv:2103.05633, which Gensyn's Verde cites). That
paper addresses verifying that training happened; this paper addresses
making model-parallel training communication-efficient enough to run over
consumer internet connections at all. Same field, different problem, kept
as separate foundation files per this repo's one-file-per-lineage rule.

Core contribution.markdown:
When a large model is split across devices (model/pipeline parallelism),
every forward and backward pass requires transferring activation and
gradient tensors between devices — tens to hundreds of MB per step — which
is fine over datacenter interconnects but becomes the binding bottleneck
over consumer internet. The paper's compression algorithm exploits a
recursive structure in transformer networks to confine activations and
gradients to a predefined low-dimensional subspace, permitting full
reconstruction in later layers. This gets up to ~100x compression on
inter-stage communication without materially altering training dynamics or
degrading convergence, which is what makes multi-participant, model-parallel
training over ordinary internet connections practical rather than purely
theoretical.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Pluralis Research's production system, Agora, uses this technique directly
as the mechanism that makes its pipeline-parallel training swarm viable —
without it, the inter-device communication cost of splitting a model across
unreliable, internet-connected consumer hardware would dominate and make
the whole approach impractical. See
[systems/pluralis-research.md](../systems/pluralis-research.md) for the
full system write-up, including the honest gap that this solves the
communication-efficiency problem but not trust/verification of contributor
honesty.

frontmatter.paper: Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in Linear Secret Sharing Schemes with a Non-Interactive Computation Phase
frontmatter.authors: Miguel de Vega, Andrei Lapets, Stanisław Jarecki, Wicher Malten, Mehmet Ugurbil, Wyatt Howe
frontmatter.venue: self-published / IACR ePrint 2023/1740 (withdrawn 2024-06-28; mirrored at nillion.pub)

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Nillion's own team announced this paper as the direct basis for their
non-interactive MPC protocol for non-linear computation — see
"Introducing the Nillion Non-Interactive MPC Protocol for Non-Linear
Computations"
(https://medium.com/@Nillion_Network/introducing-the-nillion-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations-67e9310ef479),
corroborated by the MPC Alliance's write-up of the same announcement
(https://www.mpcalliance.org/blog/nillion-introduces-a-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations).
Four of the six listed authors (de Vega, Malten, Ugurbil, and one more)
are Nillion staff — this is effectively the project publishing its own
core protocol paper, which is about the strongest grounding available
for a "foundational paper" claim in this exercise.

Core contribution.markdown:
Classic linear secret sharing schemes (LSSS) handle addition of shared
secrets for free but need rounds of communication between parties to
handle multiplication — the operation needed for anything non-linear.
This paper describes a way to evaluate arithmetic sum-of-products
expressions (sums of products of shared values — covers the multiply
step) using a **preprocessing phase that doesn't depend on the private
inputs**, so the actual computation-on-private-data step becomes
non-interactive. In plain terms: move the expensive "parties have to
talk to each other" part of secure multiplication to a setup phase that
can happen before anyone's real data is involved, so the live computation
is faster and doesn't require synchronous coordination between nodes.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
This is the specific technique underneath Nillion's **Curl** protocol,
which extends LSSS to support the non-linear math (division, square
roots, trig, logarithms) that ML workloads need but plain secret sharing
can't do cheaply. It's the piece that lets Nillion's MPC layer process
more than just linear operations on encrypted data, which is the gap
between "toy secret sharing demo" and "can actually run ML inference
on shared data."

Open question for future monitoring.markdown:
The paper was withdrawn from IACR ePrint (2023/1740, withdrawn
2024-06-28) and now only exists as a Nillion-hosted PDF. No public
explanation found for the withdrawal. If a future paper-watch run
surfaces commentary on *why* it was withdrawn (correction vs. priority
dispute vs. something substantive), that's worth a dedicated note since
it bears directly on how much to trust this as the field's seed paper.

frontmatter.paper: opML: Optimistic Machine Learning on Blockchain
frontmatter.authors: KD Conway, Cathie So, Xiaohang Yu, Kartin Wong

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Directly grounded, team's-own-paper case — about as strong as this
exercise's grounding gets. Two of the four authors are ORA's own
founding team: **Kartin Wong** (ORA co-founder, ex-Google/TikTok
infrastructure engineer) and **Cathie So** (ORA's Chief Scientist, ex-
Ethereum Foundation zkML researcher). KD Conway is credited elsewhere as
"the author of opML." This isn't a system citing outside research — it's
the system's own team publishing the paper that defines the mechanism
the system runs. (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17555)

Core contribution.markdown:
Proposes an alternative to zkML for verifying ML inference on-chain:
instead of a cryptographic proof of correct execution (expensive to
generate for large models), accept the result **optimistically** and
only pay the verification cost if someone challenges it. Borrows the
dispute structure from optimistic rollups — a bisection game narrows a
disagreement down to one contested computation step, which then gets
resolved on-chain by a Fraud Proof VM. Security rests on an "AnyTrust"
assumption: as long as at least one honest, economically-incentivized
validator is watching and willing to dispute a bad result within the
challenge window, incorrect inference gets caught. This trades zkML's
stronger cryptographic guarantee for much lower cost and the ability to
run genuinely large models (the paper demonstrates 7B-parameter LLaMA)
without circuit-compilation overhead.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
See [systems/ora-protocol.md](../systems/ora-protocol.md). ORA's
On-Chain AI Oracle (OAO) is opML's reference production deployment: ORA
nodes (running the "Tora" client) execute inference off-chain and post
results on-chain; disputes resolve through the exact bisection +
Fraud-Proof-VM mechanism this paper defines. A related ORA-authored
paper, "opp/ai: Optimistic Privacy-Preserving AI on Blockchain" (Cathie
So et al., arXiv 2402.15006), extends the same optimistic-dispute idea
to add privacy — worth a look if a future watch run tracks privacy-
preserving variants of this lineage specifically.

frontmatter.paper: Practical Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
frontmatter.authors: Keith Bonawitz, Vladimir Ivanov, Ben Kreuter, Antonio Marcedone, H. Brendan McMahan, Sarvar Patel, Daniel Ramage, Aaron Segal, Karn Seth

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Grounded via a direct citation, not inference: Google's own 2017 federated
learning announcement
([research.google/blog](https://research.google/blog/federated-learning-collaborative-machine-learning-without-centralized-training-data/))
links to this exact paper when describing "a Secure Aggregation protocol
that uses cryptographic techniques so that a coordinating server need
only combine encrypted data from hundreds or thousands of users." It's the
specific crypto contribution underneath Google's federated learning
deployments, distinct from the plain ML algorithm (Federated Averaging,
see `/systems/google-confidential-federated-learning.md`).

Core contribution.markdown:
A protocol letting a server compute the *sum* of values held by many
clients (e.g. their model-update vectors) without learning any individual
client's value — only the aggregate. It's built from secret-sharing and
pairwise-masking: each client masks its value with random numbers shared
pairwise with other clients such that the masks cancel out exactly when
all values are summed, revealing the sum but nothing about any individual
contribution. The protocol is also fault-tolerant to clients dropping out
mid-protocol (a real concern on mobile devices), which earlier secure-sum
constructions generally weren't designed to handle well at this scale.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
This is the cryptographic mechanism that lets Google's federated learning
systems claim the server never sees an individual device's model update —
only the aggregate across many devices. The later TEE-based "Confidential
Federated Computations" work (2024) layers additional server-side
confidentiality on top of this, authored by overlapping people (Bonawitz
and McMahan both appear on both papers), but Secure Aggregation is the
earlier, foundational crypto piece specifically for the aggregation step
itself. See `/systems/google-confidential-federated-learning.md` for how
the two layers relate.

was performed correctly, with two properties that distinguish it from
earlier SNARK constructions (like the PLONK lineage in

Core contribution.markdown:
Introduces the sum-check protocol: an interactive proof technique that
lets a prover convince a verifier that the sum of a multivariate
polynomial's evaluations over a Boolean hypercube equals a claimed
value, in a way that's exponentially cheaper to verify than to
brute-force. This became foundational to a large family of later
succinct arguments (GKR and its descendants) because it gives a cheap,
general-purpose way to verify a computation's structure algebraically,
without needing a trusted setup for the sum-check step itself.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
DeepProve uses sum-check (plus lookup arguments) to verify individual
LLM operators — attention, layer norm, grouped-query attention, rotary
positional embeddings — directly, rather than compiling the entire
model into one monolithic arithmetic circuit the way PLONKish systems
(like EZKL/Halo2) do. This operator-level verification approach is
part of why DeepProve claims to avoid the quadratic circuit-size blowup
that limited earlier zkML attempts at whole-model proofs. See
`systems/lagrange-labs.md` for the full system entry and its open
follow-up items.

This is as close to "grounded" as the chain gets without EZKL citing PLONK by name itself.

Core contribution.markdown:
PLONK introduced a practical, universal (not circuit-specific) SNARK
construction: a single structured reference string works for *any*
circuit up to a size bound, instead of needing a fresh trusted setup
per circuit (as earlier SNARKs like the original Groth16/Pinocchio
pipeline required). It does this via a permutation argument over
Lagrange-basis polynomials to enforce wiring constraints between gates,
combined with a polynomial commitment scheme (originally KZG) to make
the whole thing non-interactive and succinct. Follow-on work extended
this base arithmetization with custom gates and lookup arguments
("UltraPLONK" / "PLONKish"), which is the specific extension Halo2
actually implements.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
EZKL inherits PLONKish arithmetization transitively through Halo2, then
additionally swaps Halo2's native commitment scheme for KZG commitments
specifically to shrink proof size and verification cost for on-chain
use (see `/systems/ezkl.md` — this specific claim is flagged inferred,
not directly quoted from an EZKL source, so re-verify before treating
it as settled). The universality property of PLONK (one SRS per size
bound, not per circuit) is part of why a general-purpose tool like
EZKL — which has to support arbitrary ONNX graphs rather than one fixed
circuit — is practical at all.
